title: North Sikkim on a Budget: How Gangtok Tours Work
meta_description: How shared and reserved North Sikkim tours from Gangtok are priced in 2025–26: seats, vehicles, lodges, Zero Point extras and where people overspend.
summary: A shared 3-day, 2-night North Sikkim tour from Gangtok costs about ₹6,000–8,000 per person with permit, vehicle seat, lodge rooms and simple meals. A whole vehicle runs ₹18,000–28,000 before hotels. Zero Point is extra. Roads have closed often since the 2023 Teesta flood, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Why almost everyone takes a package
paras: North Sikkim is not a place you can wander into with a backpack and a bus ticket. Indian visitors need a North Sikkim permit for Lachung, Yumthang, Zero Point, Lachen and Gurudongmar, and that permit is applied for by a registered tour operator in Gangtok, not by you at a counter. Private cars from outside Sikkim are generally stopped well short of the high valleys. So the trip comes as a package: an agent arranges the permit, puts you in a locally registered vehicle with a driver who knows the road, and books a room and meals in Lachen or Lachung.

That sounds expensive, and it can be. But the package is also the cheapest way in, because the vehicle is the biggest single cost and you can share it with strangers. We have sent students, couples and families north on shared tours for years, and the price per head is close to what a few nights in Gangtok would cost anyway. The trick is knowing what you are buying.

sections.heading: Shared tours and reserved vehicles
paras: A shared tour, often called a group or seat-in-coach tour in Gangtok, sells you one seat in a Sumo, Bolero or similar jeep that the agent fills with eight to ten people. Several agents pool their customers, so you may not meet your co-travellers until the morning you leave. Everyone gets the same itinerary, the same lodge and the same set meals. If the jeep does not fill, the agent may move you to another agent's vehicle or delay you a day.

A reserved tour hires the whole vehicle for your group. You choose the departure day and the size of car, from a Bolero or Xylo to a Scorpio or Innova, and you can add a night or drop a sightseeing point. Hotels may be bundled in or booked separately. For four to six people travelling together, a reserved vehicle with simple lodges often costs only a little more per head than shared seats, and you gain control over timings, which matters at altitude.

sections.heading: What a tour costs in 2025–26
paras: These are indicative prices from typical Gangtok agent offers for budget and mid-range travel. They rise in May, during Durga Puja and Diwali, and over Christmas and New Year, and fall in the monsoon when tours run at all. Always ask whether a price is per person or per vehicle, and whether the permit, Zero Point and Gurudongmar are included.

sections.heading: What the lodge part really means
paras: In a shared tour the lodge is chosen by the agent, and it is usually a plain family hotel or homestay in Lachung or Lachen with a double or triple room, an attached bathroom, a heavy quilt and hot water by bucket or geyser. Dinner is rice, dal, a vegetable, often egg or chicken curry, and breakfast is bread, eggs or puri with tea. On the Gurudongmar morning the lodge packs tea and a simple breakfast for the 3–4 am start.

If you want a heater, a view room or a particular property, say so before paying and expect ₹500–2,000 more per room per night. Upgrading to a resort in Lachung such as Yarlam can cost several times the shared price for a place you reach at dusk and leave at dawn. Our advice for most budgets: take the standard lodge, pay for a heater in winter, and spend the difference on a second night in Lachung instead.

sections.heading: How to book without overpaying
paras: Arrive in Gangtok at least one full day before you want to go north. Permits are processed a day ahead, and the agent needs a copy of a government photo ID and two passport photographs for each person; foreign nationals need passport and visa copies for a Protected Area Permit. Shop around two or three registered agents on and near MG Marg, compare what is written on the receipt, and pay a deposit rather than the full amount if you can.

Online booking before you reach Sikkim works too, but it often adds a margin and gives you less room to change dates when a road closes. Since the October 2023 Teesta flood and the South Lhonak lake burst, the Lachen and Gurudongmar side has closed for long spells while Lachung stayed open, and the reverse has also happened. Ask the agent which points are actually permitted that week and check current status before you travel.
list: Get in writing: permit included, number of nights, which village each night, meals included, Zero Point and Gurudongmar status.
Ask what happens if a road closes: refund, rescheduled date or a Lachung-only trip at a lower price.
Keep receipts with the agent's registration name and phone number.
Carry all the cash you need for three days plus a margin; ATMs up north can be empty.

sections.heading: A sample shared tour budget
paras: Here is what one person spends on a typical shared 3-day, 2-night loop from Gangtok, Lachen first, in a normal week. It does not include getting to Gangtok from Siliguri, which adds ₹300–450 a seat each way by shared jeep on NH10, or more by the longer road through Lava and Pedong when NH10 is shut. The total lands around ₹8,000–10,500 a person, everything included.
list: Coat and boot rental for Gurudongmar and Yumthang: ₹300–800.
Tea, Maggi and toilets at Thangu, Yumthang and Zero Point stalls: ₹200–400.
One oxygen can, shared with a friend: ₹250–450.
Zero Point share if your group of eight adds it: ₹400–600.

sections.heading: Cheaper ways to see North Sikkim
paras: If even a shared tour is beyond your budget, you can still see a good part of North Sikkim without one. Kabi Lungchok, Phodong and Labrang monasteries, Mangan and Singhik need no permit for Indians and are reached by shared jeep from Gangtok's Vajra stand for ₹80–300 a seat. A night at Singhik, looking across the Teesta gorge to Kanchenjunga, costs ₹1,500–3,000 a room. Dzongu homestays at about ₹1,800–2,500 per person with all meals give you two or three days in the Lepcha reserve for less than the price of a tour, once you have the Dzongu permit. Roads here closed too after the 2023 flood, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Where people overspend
paras: Most budget leaks on this trip are small and avoidable. These are the ones we see every season.
list: Buying jackets and gumboots in Gangtok when Lachung and Lachen rent them for ₹100–300 a day.
Paying for Zero Point in advance when snow or a closure may make it impossible; agree to pay on the spot if it opens.
Booking a resort for a single night when a standard lodge does the same job for one sleep.
Taking a 2-night trip in peak week without a room fixed, then paying whatever is left.
Booking north the day after arriving in Gangtok from the plains, then losing the trip when the permit is not ready.

faqs.q: How much does a shared North Sikkim tour cost per person?
faqs.a: About ₹6,000–8,000 per person for the shared 3-day, 2-night tour from Gangtok to Lachen and Lachung, including permit, a seat in the vehicle, two nights in a basic lodge, dinner and breakfast. A 2-day Lachung-only trip costs ₹3,500–4,500. Prices rise in May, October and late December. These are indicative 2025–26 figures; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to book a North Sikkim tour in Gangtok or online?
faqs.a: Usually in Gangtok. Registered agents near MG Marg sell shared seats directly, and you can compare two or three offers in an hour. Online sellers often add a margin and are slower to adjust when a road closes. The catch is time: arrive in Gangtok at least a day early so the agent can process your permit.

faqs.q: What is included in a North Sikkim package?
faqs.a: Normally the permit, the vehicle and driver, lodge rooms in Lachen or Lachung, dinner and breakfast. Road lunches, Zero Point, coat and boot rental, oxygen cans and tips are usually extra. Ask for a written list that names each night's village and states whether Gurudongmar and Zero Point are included and open that week.

faqs.q: How much does a reserved car for North Sikkim cost?
faqs.a: Roughly ₹18,000–28,000 per vehicle for the 3-day, 2-night Lachen and Lachung loop, depending on the car size and season, with hotels usually extra. For four to six people this can be close to the shared price per head and gives you your own timings. Zero Point adds ₹3,000–4,500 per vehicle.

faqs.q: Does a shared tour leave every day?
faqs.a: In season, yes, most days, because agents pool their customers to fill vehicles. In January, February and the monsoon, fewer people travel and you may wait a day for a full jeep. Road closures since the 2023 flood also cancel departures at short notice, so keep a buffer day and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Zero Point worth the extra cost?
faqs.a: For people who have never seen deep snow, often yes: Yumesamdong sits at about 4,700 m and stays white well into May. It costs ₹3,000–4,500 per vehicle, which is small per head in a full jeep. Skip it if anyone is struggling with the altitude, and do not prepay in case snow or a closure stops the vehicle.

faqs.q: Can I get a refund if the North Sikkim road closes?
faqs.a: It depends on the agent, which is why you should ask before paying. Some refund the unused part, some move you to another date, and some switch you to a Lachung-only trip. Permit fees are rarely refunded. Get the policy written on your receipt, especially in May, June and the monsoon months.

faqs.q: Can students do North Sikkim on a low budget?
faqs.a: Yes, on a shared tour. Plan on about ₹8,000–10,500 per person for the full 3-day loop with rentals and road meals, plus jeep fares to and from Gangtok. Travel in March, early April or November to avoid peak prices, share a triple room, and rent coats in Lachung rather than buying them.

faqs.q: Do I need to tip the driver on a North Sikkim tour?
faqs.a: It is not required, but it is common and appreciated. Drivers on this route start at 3 am for Gurudongmar and handle one of the hardest roads in India. Groups often pool ₹200–500 per person for a 3-day trip, given at the end. Tip more if the driver helped with a sick traveller or a long delay.
